text: The brake you didn't ask for.
Some people take two sips of beer and turn bright red. Face, neck, sometimes the whole chest. Heart rate up. Slightly miserable.
That's not simply a low tolerance. That's a gene called A L D H two, missing a step.

Alcohol gets broken down in two stages. First into acetaldehyde, which is genuinely toxic. Then into something harmless. A L D H two runs that second stage. In people carrying the common reduced-function variant, stage two slows dramatically, and the acetaldehyde piles up.
Your body isn't rejecting the drink. It's stuck halfway through cleaning it up.
Roughly five hundred and sixty million people carry it.
And it looks like a gift. Carriers are far less likely to develop alcohol dependence. Drinking is unpleasant, so most of them don't do much of it. A brake installed at the factory.

Now the part that matters. Acetaldehyde isn't just uncomfortable. It's a recognized carcinogen. Carriers who drink regularly anyway, pushing past the brake, have a substantially higher risk of esophageal cancer than people who process alcohol normally.
So this one isn't a superpower. It's a warning light that a lot of people have learned to read as a personality trait.
If you flush, you already knew you flush. What's worth knowing is what it's telling you.
That one decides what happens after a drink. The next one decides what happens after dinner with the wrong shellfish.
